item.title: Inside House Democrats’ Report Calling For Special Counsel Probe Into Trump’s Ties To Epstein
item.description:
Earlier this week, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released a report entitled “‘We Have Certain Things in Common, Jeffrey’: The Case Against Donald Trump Emerging in the Epstein Files and DOJ’s Desperate Efforts to Cover It Up.” The report, which is over 50 pages, claims that President Donald Trump was “an active participant in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of young women during the mid-to-late 1990s” and that the DOJ and FBI are covering up his alleged connections to the disgraced financier. Trump has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing related to Epstein. Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA), a member of the House Judiciary Committee, joined “Forbes Newsroom” to discuss the report.

item.title: Who Is Melissa Highsmith? Inside The Story Of ‘Baby’ Reunited With Family 51 Years After Abduction
item.description:
On August 23, 1971, Melissa Highsmith was just a toddler when she was taken from her Fort Worth home by someone posing as a babysitter. She vanished seemingly without a trace and was missing for over 50 years. But with the help of DNA testing—and her family’s determination—she was found in 2022 and reunited with loved ones she didn’t even know she had. In the podcast “Baby,” Melissa is telling her story of what happened in those 51 years when, unbeknownst to her, she was a missing person. Sean Kipe, the host and producer of “Baby: The Melissa Highsmith Story” joined “Forbes True Crime” to discuss the show.

item.title: These 5 Senators Collectively Have Millions Riding On The AI Data Center Boom
item.description:
The data center boom is reshaping America fast: billions of dollars in land, steel, electricity and silicon, all feeding the race to advance artificial intelligence. It’s also becoming a political flashpoint. Two thirds of Americans oppose data center construction in their communities, and local backlashes to new AI infrastructure are roiling races up and down the ballot, from Senate to city council. For some elected officials, the boom is personal in another way: Their stock portfolios are riding on it. Forbes reporter Kyle Khan-Mullins joined "Forbes Newsroom" to discuss his reporting.
